ety: From Armenian ամիրա (amira), from Old Armenian ամիրայ (amiray), from Classical Syriac ܐܡܝܪܐ (ʾămīrāʾ), from Arabic أَمِير (ʔamīr, “commander”). Doublet of amir, Amir, emir, and admiral.

senses: One who digs or works on dykes; a ditcher.

In full knave noddy: the jack or knave playing card.
In full noddy-fifteen: a certain card game related to cribbage.
ety: Noun etymology 1 sense 1 is possibly from nod (“to incline the head up and down; to gradually fall asleep”) + -y (suffix forming diminutive nouns or familiar names); or a shortening of noddypoll, an obsolete alteration of hoddypoll (“fumbling, inept person”). The origin of noun etymology 1 sense 2 is uncertain; it is possibly derived from etymology 1 sense 1. Compare muggins (“fool, idiot; card game based on building in suits or matching exposed cards, the object being to get rid of one’s cards”). ety: From age + -ism. Coined by American academic Robert N. Butler in 1969.

Cooked gratin; baked in a typical type of sauce, usually with cheese, as a casserole, e.g. scalloped potatoes; scalloped corn
Baked in a scallop shell.
ety: From scallop + -ed. In culinary sense, originally referred to a seafood dish baked and served in a scallop shell, but now used more generally.

ety: After Henriette Sontag (1806–1854), German soprano singer.

ety: From German Spritzer (“splash, spatter”). By surface analysis, spritz + -er; more at spritz.

senses: Tending to obfuscate; intended to conceal the truth by confusion.
examples: I can't vote for a resolution with such obfuscatory language.

senses: Agitation; the state of being perturbed.
A small change in a physical system, or more broadly any definable system (such as a biological or economic system).
ety: Borrowed from Middle French perturbation, from Old French perturbacion, from Latin perturbatio.
examples: But her mind had never been in such perturbation; and it needed a very strong effort to appear attentive and cheerful till the usual hour of separating allowed her the relief of quiet reflection.

senses: The presentation (and subsequent interpretation) of a dramatic narrative.
examples: Is any of this true? Do we create ourselves? Is the narrativity view a profound and universal insight into the human condition?

senses: Toward the head; in bipeds such as humans, this direction corresponds to superior.
Headlike; cephaloid.
ety: From Middle French céphalique, from Latin cephalicus (“head”), from Ancient Greek κεφαλικός (kephalikós, “capital”), from κεφαλή (kephalḗ, “head”).

senses: Mineral materials.
A treatise on mineralogy.
ety: From New Latin minerālogia, from Medieval Latin minera (“mineral”) + Latin -logia (“study”). By surface analysis, mineral + -logy.

senses: An Ancient Greek nobleman.
A shop that sells cooked or prepared foods ready for serving.
ety: First attested 1864. From German Delikatessen, plural of Delikatesse (“delicacy, fine food”), at the time also spelled Delicatesse(n), from French délicatesse, from délicat (“fine”), from Latin delicatus (“alluring”). The sense of store is more recent, originating in ellipsis from the common attributive use, as in delicatessen shop, delicatessen store, etc.

senses: choroidal effusion
One who is within the domain or protection of the law.
ety: From Middle English inlaghe, inlage, from the verb (see above).

senses: A dominating leader or force, especially that which dominates a separate political entity; a hegemonist.
ety: From Ancient Greek ἡγεμών (hēgemṓn, “a leader, guide, commander, chief”), from ἡγέομαι (hēgéomai, “to lead”).

senses: An intelligent man-sized beast with varying characteristics.
A cup-shaped or dome-shaped object.
ety: Borrowed from Latin cūpula, from cūpa + -ula. Doublet of cupola. False cognate of English cupule in which English cup is descendant of Old English copp of Germanic origin.

senses: A throwing weapon made of weights on the ends of interconnected cords, designed to capture animals by entangling their legs.
A sticky thread whirled around by certain spiders to catch prey.
ety: Borrowed from Spanish bola(s) (“ball(s)”) and Portuguese bola(s) (“ball(s)”). First attested in 1843.

senses: Having occurred or having been inflicted before death.
ety: Learned borrowing from Latin ante mortem (“before death”).
examples: Although the antemortem injuries are severe, they are not the cause of death.

senses: coarse linen fabric
A person who removes muck (waste, debris, broken rock, etc.), especially from a mine, construction site, or stable.
ety: By surface analysis, muck + -er. Compare Swedish mokare/mockare (“one who cleans dung”, agent noun) → rörmokare/rörmockare (“plumber”, literally “pipe mucker”). Compare the military sense to Finnish mokkeri (“private”, colloquial), to Swedish mocka (“to clean muck”); and Swedish mecka/meka (“to repair or improve (mechanical) equipment”), to meckaniker (“mechanic”); also Swedish mucka (“to complete military service”), from Tavringer Romani mucka (“to be released”). The military sense might also derive from a slur, a common practice in military lingo.

senses: To enclose within a cyst.
To be enclosed within a cyst.
The principle, state or quality of being illiberal.
examples: As the Oxford political theorist Michael Freeden observed, if just one of the necessary components — for example, the free market — dominates, then the result can be illiberalism.
In the Netherlands, the anti-immigrant right became the second-most-popular vote-getter — a new high-water mark for illiberalism in that once famously liberal country.

senses: An aspergillum.
A ceremonial herb bundle or perforated object used to sprinkle witch's water at the commencement of a ritual.
ety: From the verb asperge, ultimately a learned borrowing from Latin aspergō.
